chapters.summary: Council staff welcome attendees to the Committee on General Welfare hearing, ask phones to be silenced, explain appearance cards, and instruct the public not to approach the dais. The chair is then invited to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens General Welfare hearing and sets decorum

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, please silence all phones.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to speak in today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with one of the sergeants.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moving forward, no one is to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Crystal Hudson welcomes attendees to the hearing on the City Family Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement, known as CityFHEPS. She introduces herself and states her pronouns.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson opens hearing on CityFHEPS legislation

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Welcome to today's hearing on legislation concerning the City Family Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement, more commonly known as City FEPS.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm Crystal Hudson, General Welfare Committee Chair, and my pronouns are she, her.

chapters.summary: Hudson describes New York City's intertwined affordable housing and homelessness crises, citing 96,528 people in shelters in July 2026, including 30,824 children. She argues the true number of unhoused New Yorkers is likely in the hundreds of thousands.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson details homelessness crisis and shelter census

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: New York City is facing two intertwined crises, an acute affordable housing shortage and a staggering number of New Yorkers who are unhoused.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: According to the Coalition for the Homeless, in July 2026, 96,528 people slept in New York City shelters each night, including 30,824 children.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The total number of people without homes is far higher.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Between folks sleeping unsheltered and people living doubled or tripled up with family or friends, the number is more likely in the hundreds of thousands.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Let that sink in.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Hundreds of thousands of our neighbors, school kids, people fleeing domestic violence, people who just can't make the rent because...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It's too damn high.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Have to question whether they will have a roof over their heads tonight.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What a wholly unacceptable state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In New York City, everyone has a right to shelter, but frankly, shelter isn't enough.

chapters.summary: Hudson says shelter is not enough and explains CityFHEPS helps New Yorkers move into and maintain permanent housing. She notes the program helped 123,762 individuals from 2018 to March 2025 and that its budget grows to $1.97 billion in fiscal year 2027.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson outlines CityFHEPS permanent housing and budget growth

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: As a city, it is imperative that we do everything we can to get people into permanent, stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: City FEPS, I'm sorry, sergeants, do you mind?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: City FEPS is one of the city's tools to do just that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: As the city's main rental assistance program, City FEPS supports New Yorkers who are in shelters or at risk of losing their homes to move into and maintain housing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: According to DSS, between the inception of City FEPS in 2018 and March 2025, the program helped 123,762 individuals secure permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Understanding the dire need for this kind of assistance, the budget for City FEPS has continually grown.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2026, the city budgeted $1.78 billion for the program.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In fiscal year 2027, that amount will rise to $1.97 billion, with even more projected for 2028 and 2029.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In short, this is an important program and one that the city invests heavily in.

chapters.summary: Hudson explains applicants and landlords face pain points accessing CityFHEPS. She previews Intros 98, 100, 101, 641, and T2026-1424, covering inspections, lease-up data, response times, payment timing, and a landlord portal.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson previews five CityFHEPS reform bills

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But the program is only valuable if people can actually access it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: To do so, New Yorkers applying for City FEPS need to be able to understand where their applications for assistance stand.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: They need to be able to find eligible apartments, move into safe and habitable homes, and receive their rental assistance.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: assistance payments reliably and on time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Landlords participating in rental assistance programs also need to be able to navigate the CityFEP's landscape.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there are pain points at each of these stages that block New Yorkers who really need the assistance from benefiting from it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The five pieces of legislation we're hearing today attempt to remove these roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro numbers 98, 100, and 101 are sponsored by my colleague, Councilmember Gail Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro number 98 is about ensuring apartments are safe before city FEPS assistance is used towards rent.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: While also balancing the need for move-ins to happen as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro number 100 would require the Department of Social Services, or DSS, to report the average time it takes for an individual to secure housing after receiving a shopping letter, a document issued by DSS that applicants use while searching for an eligible apartment.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro number 101 focuses on the time it takes DSS to respond to an application for a CityFEPS voucher.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer may give a statement later about her legislation.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Intro number 641, sponsored by Councilmember Ressler, addresses the timing of rental assistance payments.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: This bill would require that DSS make CityFEP's rental assistance payments no later than seven days before the first day of the month to which the payment applies.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Timely payments are important not only for tenants, but also for landlords who participate in the program.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Payment delays can create uncertainty for both sides and can undermine the stability CityFEP is intended to provide.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: He also may give a statement later.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Finally, pre-considered intro number T2026-1424, sponsored by Councilmember Murano,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: seeks to make the CityFEPS process smoother for landlords by requiring DSS to administer an online portal for landlords who participate in rental subsidy programs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: He also may make a statement later.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from the administration and the public about these proposals.

chapters.summary: Hudson thanks committee staff and her own staff for their work on the hearing. She then hands the proceeding to committee counsel to administer the oath to the administration witnesses.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson thanks committee staff and transitions to oath

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I want to conclude by thanking the committee staff for their work on this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Hannah Cohn, Penina Rosenberg, Justin Campos, Faridha Rahman, and Elizabeth Childers-Garcia.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank my staff, Andrew Wright, Elika Runtan, and Demi Brown.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I will now pass it over to the committee council to administer the oath to the administration.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.title: Council staff administers affirmation to mayoral administration witnesses

utterances.text: Now in accordance with the rules of the council, I will administer the affirmation to the witnesses from the mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

chapters.summary: Erin Dalton identifies herself as Commissioner of the Department of Social Services. She introduces HRA Administrator Scott French and Executive Deputy Commissioner Andrea Reed.
chapters.title: DSS Commissioner Erin Dalton introduces herself and colleagues

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: My name is Erin Dalton, and I'm the Commissioner of the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Hudson and members of the Committee on General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm Erin Dalton, and I serve as the Commissioner of the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Joining me today are HRA Administrator Scott French and Andrea Reed, Executive Deputy Commissioner of Housing Services Administration at HRA.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for convening today's legislative hearing and offering me the opportunity to provide feedback on the five legislative proposals on the agenda for today.

chapters.summary: Dalton thanks the committee for the hearing and says DSS appreciates constructive dialogue on legislation. She notes the agency looks forward to continuing conversations with bill sponsors.
chapters.title: Dalton thanks council and cites ongoing legislative dialogue

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I want to begin by expressing my appreciation for our ongoing constructive dialogue on legislation and legislative proposals.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: To the extent that legislative proposals can benefit from more nuanced, detailed understandings of current practice and the impacts of these proposals, we look forward to continuing these conversations with the bill sponsors.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Turning to the central topic of today's hearing, CityFAPS.

chapters.summary: Dalton says CityFHEPS was established in November 2018 and now serves more than 71,000 households and 162,000 New Yorkers. She calls it part of a continuum of care and urges continued federal and state investment.
chapters.title: Dalton describes CityFHEPS history and scale

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: CityFAPS was established in November of 2018 with the consolidation of several predecessor housing voucher programs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Today, CityFAPS serves more than 71,000 households and 162,000 New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: CityFAPS serves as a component of a continuum of care that sets vulnerable New Yorkers on a path towards permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: While I am grateful to live and work in a city that cares for its vulnerable neighbors in this way, it is worth reminding us all that CityFAPS is one of several rental subsidies established to support

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: low-income people in need of housing assistance.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I urge us all to continue to advocate for federal and state housing and rental subsidy investments, which have been cut considerably in recent years.

chapters.summary: Dalton says the bills aim to improve timeliness, customer service, and transparency, which align with administration goals. She describes DSS moves to single staff review, supervisory approval, and streamlined eligibility focus to reduce return packages.
chapters.title: Dalton outlines DSS government efficiency and process improvements

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Briefly, before turning to the specific legislation on the agenda today, I would like to take a moment to share the agency and administration's perspective on government efficiency and government excellence, which is at the heart of each of the bills being discussed today.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The intent of each of the bills is to improve timeliness, customer service, and transparency of this critical government program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This is a key pillar of the administration, demonstrated in numerous ways, but explicitly by aiming to accelerate the housing development and move-in process by issuing the speed report announced in May this year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Likewise, at DSS, we have taken steps to improve CityFEP's review and approval process, including shifting to a single staff review and supervisory approval for DHS cases and fine-tuning our focus on eligibility for property,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: ownership, payee, subsidy type, and clients.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Through increased staff and provider training and landlord engagement, our goal is that the streamlining of the process will result in fewer return packages and a reduction in the time it takes for clients to move into permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I now turn to the legislation on the agenda today.

chapters.summary: Dalton says Intro 98 would require the Commissioner of Social Services to deem a dwelling habitable before approving CityFHEPS rental assistance. She shares the goal of safe housing but says DSS opposes some specific requirements and has operated a nine-month pilot.
chapters.title: Dalton addresses Intro 98 habitability inspections and pilot program

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 98, sponsored by Councilmember Brewer, would require the Commissioner of Social Services to deem a dwelling unit habitable before

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: approving City FEPS rental assistance for that unit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: All New Yorkers deserve safe and affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We share the goal of ensuring that City FEPS inspections are conducted quickly and result in safe, quality housing for the New Yorkers we serve.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: While we oppose some of the specific requirements of the legislation, we are pleased to report on a pilot program that we think meets the intent of Introduction 98.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For the last nine months, we've been operating a pilot program that tests many of the approaches articulated in the proposed legislation.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We believe that the lessons from this pilot program set forth the foundation for an approach that balances the desire to process applications quickly with the need for safe housing conditions.

chapters.summary: Dalton explains the pilot uses provider inspections for most units and HRA inspectors for difficult units, with virtual re-inspections via WhatsApp or FaceTime. She warns Intro 98 as drafted could limit flexibility, increase burden, and require more HRA inspectors.
chapters.title: Dalton details inspection pilot, virtual reviews, and concerns with Intro 98

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: This process allows for inspections to be conducted by providers in most instances and HRA inspectors for more challenging units.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are also exploring the establishment of a pre-qualified list of third-party inspectors to allow approved organizations to inspect and approve vacant apartments prior to occupancy for all newly constructed buildings.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Like the proposed legislation, our approach now distinguishes between minor and major repairs, and our expedited re-inspection process offers an opportunity to promptly remedy minor faults and relay that evidence to HRA of the fix.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Landlords may send photos documenting that the failures have been addressed and that the unit now meets habitability standards.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Virtual inspections have proven to be a valuable tool in both maintaining agency safety and habitability standards,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: and from an efficiency perspective.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: HRA uses virtual inspections and or uses virtual inspections for re-inspection using WhatsApp or FaceTime to help streamline the process further.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We will be ready to roll out these process improvements system-wide in the first quarter of next year.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: While unintended, if adopted as drafted, this bill would limit our flexibility, increase burden and time to process, and require the addition of many more HRA inspectors and inspections.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are committed to responsible and expedited approval, move in timeliness for CityFAPS clients, and we think the current process well balances the joint goals of processing quickly and ensuring safe housing for New Yorkers we serve.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We look forward to the discussion of the proposed legislation and changes we've made to the process and hope they meet the underlying goals of the proposed legislation.

chapters.summary: Dalton says Intro 100 would require annual reporting on average time to secure housing after receiving a voucher. She supports transparency but wants further discussion on metric interpretation and notes factors like low vacancy rates and geographic constraints.
chapters.title: Dalton discusses Intro 100 lease-up time reporting

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 100, sponsored by Councilmember Brewer, would require the Department of Social Services to

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: annually submit to the Mayor and the Speaker of the Council and to include in the Mayor's Management Report the average time it takes for an individual to secure housing after receiving a voucher.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We share the aim of advancing transparency through timely and accurate reporting of relevant data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are able to report on the metric proposed in the legislation, but we hope to have further discussion with the bill sponsor around the interpretation of these metrics and whether they are the best metrics to use to assess the CityFEP's program.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There are numerous factors impacting timelines from time of receipt of an issue.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: shopping letter to move out, including a historically low vacancy rate for affordable permanent housing units.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For instance, a survivor of domestic violence may be limited geographically to ensure safety.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Another household may be focused on finding housing in a particular borough due to the location of their child's school and health services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition to the challenges posed by attempting to gain general insights from a nuanced metric, DSS already reports on various metrics, including Local Law 79, length of stay reporting

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: for rental assistance programs, and we would like to explore whether the sponsor feels the benefit of, explore with the sponsor the benefit of adding this additional metric.

chapters.summary: Dalton says Intro 101 would require DSS to respond to CityFHEPS applications within 15 days. She reports average processing time improved from 28 days to 24.8 days and says a client-facing Access HRA portal update coming in October will improve transparency.
chapters.title: Dalton discusses Intro 101 15-day application response requirement

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 101, sponsored by Councilmember Burrow, would require the Department of Social Services to respond to CityFEP's rental assistance applications within 15 days

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: of receipt to inform the applicant of whether the application has been approved, denied, or requires correction or additional information.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We understand the legislation's aim of processing applications in a timely manner and to keep applicants informed.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our average processing time for CityFAPS, defined as the time of submission to the complete package of approval, is 28 days, which has improved over the last month or month and a half to 24.8 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Currently, clients are informed about their application status by case managers at biweekly independent living.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Plan check-ins.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In addition, by the end of October,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We will be able to release an improvement to the Access HRA client-facing portal where CityFEP's application status will be posted and available to clients.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We believe that taken together, these enhancements meet the goal of the legislation in providing timely and transparent information on the status of CityFEP's applications.

chapters.summary: Dalton says Intro 641 would require payments no later than seven days before the month to which they apply. DSS currently issues payment on the 26th, with EFT within 24 hours and paper checks around the first; state shelter allowance payments are split and outside DSS control.
chapters.title: Dalton discusses Intro 641 rental assistance payment timing

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Introduction 641, sponsored by Councilmember Ressler, would require that DSS issue CityFEP's rental assistance payments no later than seven days before the first day of the month to which the payment will be applied.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: DSS currently issues payment on the 26th of the month prior to when the payment is applied.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For landlords enrolled in the electronic fund transfer, they will receive this funding within 24 hours of that day.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And for those who still opt to receive a paper check, they will receive it in or on around the first of the month.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We believe this is a reasonable approach that is working well.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That said, we understand that landlords do not just receive rental payments from the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For some tenants, rental contributions are made from New York State's welfare management system, which issues a shelter allowance payment in two parts, at the beginning of the month and in the middle of the month.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: While we understand that this may be frustrating to landlords, DSS cannot change how or when the state issues those payments.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Also, DSS is very clear with landlords up front about the state payment system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Landlords agree to the terms in the CityFAPS payment structure on the outset, acknowledging and writing being a written

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: signed agreement that payments received within the month are considered timely.

chapters.summary: Dalton says DSS agrees with providing landlords a user-friendly portal and has already launched ServiceNow, the NYC Landlord Portal, and Apartment Offers Portal. She says the bill's January 2027 deadline is not feasible and more lead time is needed.
chapters.title: Dalton discusses T2026-1424 landlord portal bill

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Pre-considered introduction file T-2026-1424, sponsored by Councilmember Marano, requires the agency to create a portal for landlords who participate in rental subsidies programs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Administered by the Department of Social Services.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We agree with the aim of providing landlords a user-friendly portal to perform important administrative functions, receive updates, and register to receive payments electronically.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's why the agency launched the ServiceNow system back in 2016 and the current New York City Landlord Portal and the Apartment Offers Portal, both launched in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Since then, we have continued to take strides in making these systems more capable of meeting landlord needs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: As written, the bill proposed the bill proposes the landlord portal and act the provisions outlined in the legislation by January of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We hope to discuss with the sponsor the significant additional lead time we would need to accomplish the elements this legislation proposes.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: While we have substantial IT work underway to pursue many of the functionalities this bill seeks to establish, we do not believe it would be feasible to have all of these functions up and running by January 2027.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For instance, today our portal allows landlords to upload some of the documents, but not all the documents they are required to submit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: At present, some documents are presented as part of the application submitted by a provider.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Over time, we plan to transition to a new system.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: transition to a system where a portal can collect all of the required documents.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Altogether, this work represents part of a larger IT build-out process that requires time set aside for testing, quality assurance, and the ultimate release that we do not see accounted for in the proposed legislation.

chapters.summary: Dalton says DSS supports the bills' intentions to improve timeliness, customer service, and transparency. She thanks the council for its leadership and welcomes questions.
chapters.title: Dalton concludes DSS supports bill intentions and welcomes questions

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: In conclusion, DSS supports the intention of the bills to improve timeliness, customer service, and transparency.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We believe that further dialogue between the agency and council will contribute to crafting targeted solutions that accomplish those goals.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I appreciate the council's leadership and attention to ensuring vulnerable New Yorkers find stable, permanent, affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I also appreciate the opportunity to testify today and welcome your questions.

chapters.summary: Hudson thanks Dalton and notes Council Members Nurse, Ung, and Morano have joined. She turns the floor to Council Member Morano for remarks on his legislation.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson thanks Dalton and recognizes attending members

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I'd like to note that we've been joined by Council Members Nurse, Ung, and Murano.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I will turn it over to Council Member Murano for remarks on his legislation.

chapters.summary: Morano thanks Chair Hudson and describes his bill as a response to landlord and tenant complaints about missing checks, wrong addresses, paperwork errors, and months of unpaid rent. He says reliable city payments are needed so landlords accept vouchers.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano remarks on his landlord portal legislation

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Commissioner, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I look forward to asking a couple of questions in a bit.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to thank everybody here, but especially Chair Hudson, for joining me as a sponsor of the legislation that we're considering today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm a Republican from Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair Hudson is a Democrat from Brooklyn, and we probably don't agree on every housing issue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But we agree on this one.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When the city promises to pay somebody's rent, it should actually pay the rent.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't think that's a particularly radical proposition.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So this legislation grew out of complaints.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: brought directly to my office by landlords and tenants who were having an extraordinarily difficult time dealing with the city's housing voucher program.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So we've heard about missing checks, payments sent to the wrong address, paperwork errors, and landlords going months without receiving money that they're legitimately owed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And when they try to get somebody at the city to fix it, they're bounced around from one office to another.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Sometimes it seems like it's easier to get a reservation at Rayo's than to get somebody on the phone to address this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But there's a serious consequence to all of this.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And it's one that results in less housing for everybody.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I really have to say that the issue of getting more people in housing they can afford shouldn't be partisan in the least.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If we want property owners to accept housing vouchers, we ought to make sure the city is a reliable partner.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: This is about helping landlords get paid, but it's also about helping tenants remain housed and making government a little less frustrating for everybody involved.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I think the fact that Chair Hudson and I are working together on this demonstrates something important.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You don't have to agree on every housing policy to agree that people deserve a functioning government.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So looking forward to hearing more from today's witnesses, particularly those who've experienced some of these problems firsthand.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to know what we're missing, what else needs to be fixed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate the commissioner's testimony touching upon a couple of areas.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

chapters.summary: Brewer says CityFHEPS is important and can save up to $635 million in shelter costs. She explains Intros 98, 100, and 101 on inspections, lease-up reporting, and 15-day responses, thanks advocates and staff, and Hudson notes recent op-eds.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer remarks on her three CityFHEPS bills, Hudson notes op-eds

utterances.text: Thank you very much for holding this hearing and for discussing this topic.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think we know how important city FEPS are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know that families who leave for permanent housing do so with city FEPS voucher and all the challenges.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know that rental assistance with vouchers could save the city up to $635 million in shelter costs, and we know how much has gone into this discussion about city FEPS.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I introduced three bills, and I want to thank women in need in particular for their support in the crafting of these bills, as well as the council staff.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Until 98 would make the inspection system more practical.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Apartments still have to be safe, but if an owner fixes a few minor problems, we do not need to send an inspector back when photos or video can show the work was done.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Serious problems would still require another inspection.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That is after much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: examples, many examples of this problem.

utterances.text: even a voucher to move into an apartment.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If people are waiting too long, we need to know what the delays are.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We certainly need the safeguards.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We need to cut unnecessary delays.

utterances.text: So thank you to Christine Quinn, Chris Mann, everybody at Wynn, and all the advocates, and certainly Cynthia Hornig and Shula Puder for my staff.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.text: And we had an op-ed on this topic yesterday in AM New York.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: And one in the Daily News.

utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

chapters.summary: Hudson begins questions on Intro 98 and asks DSS to walk through its current habitability inspection process. Dalton defers to Executive Deputy Commissioner Andrea Reed.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DSS on current habitability inspection process

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I will jump into questions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So could you, for Intro 98, in relation to the procedure for determining that a dwelling unit is habitable for the purposes of the City FEPS program, could you walk us through the current process DSS follows when conducting

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: habitability?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Habitability inspections.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Say that three times fast.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I had to say it twice in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to turn that one over to the Executive Deputy Commissioner Reed.

chapters.summary: Reed describes a two-step process: a pre-clearance review of housing and building code violations across HPD, DOB, FDNY, and Finance, followed by a physical or video walkthrough. Providers conduct most inspections, while HRA handles units most likely to fail.
chapters.title: Andrea Reed explains two-step habitability assessment

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Good afternoon, council members.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If you could just pull the microphone down just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah, there you go.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We share the goal of safety and habitability assessment, and we take that process very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The safety and habitability assessment is a two-step process consisting of a standardized preclearance process and then a standardized walkthrough process.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The pre-cleaning process consists of an online review of housing units and building codes violations and other information and databases

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: with New York City agencies, including HPD, which is Housing Preservation and Development, DOB, Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The fire department, FDNY, and also the Department of Finance, where we check for ownership information and HPD for unit building registration information.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Once all those checklist items are conducted and there's a pass clearance, then it requires a physical inspection.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Physical inspections can be done by video and or in person.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Both the provider and HRA conduct those inspections.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: HRA conduct the inspections that are for those units that are most likely not to pass the legal standards, and those are units in cellars, basements, attics, and first floors.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The other inspections are done by the provider agency.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: There's a standard...

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Checklist is called the apartment review checklist and that both providers and HRA use that to conduct those inspections.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how long it takes to schedule a walkthrough and what percentage of unit inspections fail. Reed says inspections are scheduled within two to three weeks and about 50% of HRA inspections fail, with about two inspections before approval.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about inspection wait times and failure rates

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is the average wait time to schedule an apartment for a walkthrough by DHS?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: In the reorganization, the inspection team now reports to HRA.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Right now, inspections are scheduled within two to three weeks.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what percent of unit inspections for habitability fail?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: For the inspections that are conducted by HRA, a good 50% of them fail.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so there's about two inspections before an application is approved for lease up.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry, there are two inspections before they're approved, did you say?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yes, about 50% fail of the ones that are conducted by HRA, the cellar, basements, attic, first floors, right?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The inspections that are conducted by the provider, we don't have that information readily available because when those units fail, the provider works with the landlord to correct those failures before the application is submitted to us.

chapters.summary: Dalton says HRA conducted about 8,509 inspections in calendar year 2025 and roughly 44% failed. She notes HRA does about one-third of all inspections, takes harder units, and the system does not collect failure data for provider inspections.
chapters.title: Dalton provides HRA inspection data and notes provider data gaps

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And, Chair, if it would be helpful, I could provide some specific data on the numbers that are done by HRA.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Would that be helpful just to give some context?

utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.text: Yeah, so when we look at calendar year 25, HRA staff did about 8,500, so 8,509 specifically.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The actual percentage was 44% there.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Approved or failed?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Failed.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So 64% were, or 66% were passing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think it does bear to mention that HRA, as already mentioned,

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: does about a third of all the inspections.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so many more are done by the providers.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Again, we take the harder ones.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So those are going to be more likely to fail.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So we think that the numbers, while we don't have the actual data for the inspections done by providers, fail far less often than the ones done by HRA, which are critical for us to do in order to ensure the safety side of this inspection process.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And sorry, you can get those numbers to us or cannot?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We do not.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Our systems do not collect that information.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: At all?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: On the provider side.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Feature enhancements down the road.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We're looking to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I mean, it would be great, obviously, to just have a sense of what's going on in the entire system, not just the portion that you all inspect.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about the anticipated cost of pre-qualified third-party inspectors for new buildings. Scott French says costs are still being developed with HPD. Hudson also asks whether virtual inspections are limited to video tools like WhatsApp and FaceTime; French confirms live walkthroughs.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions third-party inspector costs and virtual inspection methods

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then before I continue my question, I do want to just go to your testimony, if I may, Commissioner, and just ask a couple of quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You mentioned with regards to Intro 98 that you're exploring the establishment of a pre-qualified list for third-party inspectors to allow approved organizations to inspect and approve vacant apartments prior to occupancy in all newly constructed buildings.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you anticipate a particular cost for that?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think that's still being developed with our partners at HPD as well, so we don't have that cost yet, but it's something that's actively being worked on.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then I want to confirm, you mentioned virtual inspections have been a valuable tool.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is that just limited to, or do you classify WhatsApp and FaceTime inspections as virtual inspections, or are there other types of virtual inspections?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Other than WhatsApp or FaceTime.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We mentioned, thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We mentioned WhatsApp and FaceTime because they're the most prevalent ones that are used.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: If you have an Android phone, everyone has WhatsApp.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, but it's all video conferencing.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I just worry with the word of virtual, that is a very broad description.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so with AI and everything else that we know is going on, I want to just make sure that it's actual video.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Software that's being used as opposed to just some sort of like virtual tool.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Yeah, we are walking through with them as they do it.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: It's virtually in regards to they're taking us through as they take the readings.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: They need to show that reading on the screen so that the staff person can look at it and affirm that the readings are within appropriate levels and those aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Yeah, it is a we're walking through together.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Just one person is virtually on the camera.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Just wanted to confirm.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what drove the improvement from 28 days to 24.8 days for application approval. Dalton and Reed explain reorganization, a shift from three-touch to two-touch review, four eligibility pillars, longer document validity, and better supervisor comments.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about Intro 101 processing improvements

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then with regards to Intro 101, you mentioned that there has been an improvement over the last month from the time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Of submission to approval going from 28 days to 24.8 days.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What do you attribute that to?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, I will let the executive deputy commissioner give a little bit more detail, but there's been a significant reorganization of resources and refocusing.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So items that were once done by both DHS and HRA are now just done with one unit in HRA.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think after the initial, of course, challenge of reorganization, we really started to make strides in making those faster.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But if you'd like to provide some additional details, that would probably be helpful.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So with the reorganization, we really tried to streamline.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: the process for application review and approval.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: As Commissioner mentioned, we went from a three-touch review to a two-touch review.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So there's one staff reviewing and one supervisor reviewing.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: But we also changed the foundational lens of how we look at the review, and we look at three eligibility, four eligibility pillars.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's the ownership eligibility, client and subsidy eligibility, and owner eligibility, so that the staffing have been trained

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: and they are now given the tools to be able to critically think and make assessments along those eligibility lens.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so in the past, applications would go back and forth for simple reasons.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Now they're able to look at those eligibility and make sure that those are being met and so the application can move forward faster.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Additionally, we changed the life of the documents.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so documents were about four months and now they're all at six months.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so less back and forth to update documents.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Once the application is submitted, those documents also freeze in their valid time frames and so no longer back and forth for new updated documents.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: In addition to that, the supervisors now have increased the comment section in the

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: electronic application, and so they're able to document whatever issues have been identified so that the providers, if we have to return the case, they know exactly what they need to do to send it.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: case back.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So we've been able to move the needle.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We're starting to see a turn.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The applications are moving faster.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The return rates have gone down.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's trending down.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I don't want to boast yet, but we're starting to see a turn.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so hopefully as we continue to advance, we will see more progress.

chapters.summary: Hudson praises the progress and asks when the streamlining and reorganization started. Reed and French say units were integrated about a year ago, with many changes rolling out over the past six months.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks when streamlining and reorganization began

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would say if there's a time to boast now would be the time.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So you should boast away.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed

utterances.speaker: Scott French

utterances.speaker: Scott French

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Several of the things the executive deputy commissioner mentioned have happened probably in the past six months or so, sort of rolling out in a way, which is why we're starting to see them cumulatively actually turn the trend to lesser days to approval.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Additional lead time that you think would be needed in order to accomplish what he's setting out to do by January of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How much time do you anticipate?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Needing in order to be ready?

utterances.text: I think we can come back with specifics.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think there are things that will roll in over time.

utterances.text: So we are actively, right, we have systems already that we utilize that engage and support landlords, right, and property owners from our sort of

utterances.text: as well as our landlord portal system, which is a way for landlords to have more insight into their payments and also receive electronic fund payments.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We are in active sort of enhancements on all of those systems right now.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Many of those enhancements actually speak to what's in the council members bill.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We can come back with specifics as to when we see different pieces of this starting to roll out with something like this.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: It's often over.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: many, many months because you try to sort of design it so you're releasing along the way rather than waiting till the end.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But we will start to see.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: additional enhancements in the first quarter of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And then periodically along that line, we can follow up with a more specific timeline and the sort of markers we think we're going to hit as it regards to the things outlined in the council members bill.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

chapters.summary: Morano notes ServiceNow and two landlord portals launched in 2016 and 2023 and asks how many systems a landlord must use. Reed says landlords use the offer system and landlord portal separately, and cannot yet see inspections, paperwork, payments, and complaints in one place.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions DSS on multiple landlord portals

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm going to go to Councilmember Murado, followed by Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, in your testimony, you mentioned ServiceNow, which launched in 2016, and two other landlord portals launched in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So by my count, we're talking about three different technology systems that have been introduced over the last decade.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many different websites, accounts, or interfaces does a landlord actually have to use today to participate in CityFEPS from beginning to end?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'm going to defer to my colleagues on that one.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So at the front end of the process, the landlord submit a unit that they're offering for rent in the offer system.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So that's one system.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: As we move along and the application is approved, the landlord now have access when they sign up for the landlord portal.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Now they're able to see their payment history, all the government payments, the subsidy payments and the shelter allowance payments.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: They're also able to submit their documents regarding signing up for EFT and the landlord portal itself.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: In the future, as Administrator Scotch mentioned, there's lots of IT advancements on the horizon where the two systems will interface.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so that.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Documents submitted on the front end will feed also the back end so that there's not multiple touch points.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So at the moment, can a landlord go to one place and see the status of their apartment inspection, their paperwork, their rental payments, and any outstanding complaints?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Not at this time.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The communication process right now is once you're in the application phase of the journey, that you're talking with your provider and they have the most up-to-date information that they can share with you.

chapters.summary: Morano asks if DSS is developing systems with one unified strategy or building new solutions piecemeal. Scott French says the systems grew up separately but are now being interfaced and unified toward a single entry point; Morano presses for a committed date, and Dalton says DSS will follow up.
chapters.title: Morano asks whether DSS is unifying landlord-facing technology systems

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I guess my motivation behind the legislation is...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And it's kind of a combination question and comment, are we developing these systems with one unified strategy?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Or are we building a new technological solution every time we discover another administrative problem?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I'll jump in there.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think these systems grew up in response to specific aspects of the process, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But I think, as I had mentioned before and what we've talked about, right, this next technological enhancement is about now interfacing and unifying those systems so that we can get to a single entry point for individuals.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: You know but as our systems and processes developed over time right certain aspects of these say the inspection aspect was developing along a certain time frame and the technology was needed there while the city FEPS

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: sort of package processing was being developed in another way but we've acknowledged and sort of see

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We now need to bring all of those together, which is why, you know, the capital projects we currently have on hand are really moving towards that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we can follow up with specifics as to, you know, how we see that working for the benefit of landlords, providers and everybody moving forward as sort of a.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Singular system one has to deal with.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Chair, may I ask one more question or should I wait to...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Only one more.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One more, yes.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So, Commissioner, you said in your testimony that the January 27 deadline in my bill isn't feasible and that you need significant additional lead time, and I appreciate you being candid about that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But this isn't a request to build a spaceship.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're talking about uploading documents.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: tracking payments and resolving complaints and functions that exist in other online services.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So let me ask you as straightforward as possible, what date can you commit to?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't have a date for you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We are happy to get back to you with specific timelines.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think we share the goal of the legislation you've introduced.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We do want to provide excellent customer service to the landlords and property managers we're working with.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Many aspects of the system are already underway, as Administrator French said, and we've probably testified to.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Some documents can be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We're working on additional, and we just have to lay out the IT infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you could get back to me with a date certain, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what challenges remain in speeding up inspections and how the pilot handles minor versus major repairs. Dalton says the pilot differentiates minor faults fixed with photos or video from major issues requiring re-inspection, and the agency plans system-wide rollout next year.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer questions DSS on inspection challenges and pilot

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Regarding Intro 98, I was next door.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're lucky you're not dealing with signal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're doing very well.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, that's what we were talking about for the last four hours.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question is, if that inspection process is what is improving from 28 to 24 days, but we'd like to make it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Less days for getting into the apartment.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What are some of the challenges?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you're working perhaps on pre-qualified for inspections.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're doing a pilot.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I would just wonder, because I do know in my, you know, not as half as experience as you or as Wynn, but people are coming in that the smallest item is keeping them from moving into that apartment.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Now, you also have...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You know, people who are mold and that's not a fixable immediately.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how does that, how can we fix that if at all?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, what is it, I assume that the inspections, no matter how hard you try, are still slowing down the process.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll start here and then my colleagues may want to jump in.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The pilot seems to have been working to achieve many of the things that you're after here, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So one of the things that we do think is important, as you could hear, we're only doing about a third of the inspection and the providers are doing the rest.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We think that's important to keep that in place.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't think you would want us to be doing all of those inspections.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So that's...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: For the staff to do it, probably.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That part we'd like to maintain.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We completely agree that there is a difference between minor faults in an inspection and more significant ones.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so through this pilot process, we have made that differentiation, and we're allowing the landlords to fix and then prove to us that they fixed the minor things

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: using that kind of video and photographic evidence to demonstrate that they fixed those.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So that's underway.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then for the more major challenges, we are then going out and re-inspecting.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I think those things in combination have started to move that process forward more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think you would also share that there is always a balance between, particularly for these more difficult units that HRA is conducting, a balance between safety and speed.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think importantly the lessons that we've learned we are about to roll out to the whole system and so for the entire system in the in the first quarter of next year we would start to see the benefits of the innovations we've put forward over the last nine months okay and what are you

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: like that two-thirds being done by the private sector, that would not be done by the third-party inspectors.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That would still be done by the owners, basically.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to figure out.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Where are the third-party folks?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: The third party goes to the last part of your introduction, which is about the new bill.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The new buildings.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, that's where they would be.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about roughly 2,000 people losing federal emergency housing vouchers. Scott French says a whole-of-administration approach with HPD and NYCHA is underway, state HAVP vouchers are coming, and the timeline rolls into the end of December.
chapters.title: Brewer asks DSS about EHV vouchers and federal funding deadline

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then the other question just quickly is, there are 2,000 people who still need vouchers, right, because they're getting kicked off of other vouchers from the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you on top of that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're going to give them all vouchers?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I'll jump in there in a second, but I think I just also want to clarify first, it's not owners doing the inspections for the other two-thirds, it's the DHS providers doing those inspections.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I just want to sort of be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Regarding the EHV, which I believe you're referring to, I believe that is sort of a whole-of-admin approach is being utilized to address that

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: need amongst those individuals.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think the...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: HPD.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: The final details are being sort of developed between us, HPD, NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: There are some, you know, vouchers from the state that are coming available, HAVP, and some other vouchers as well.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I think the admin is very much focused on the housing stability of those households at risk.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But it is something that's being done across.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have a November deadline?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I believe it's the end of December is where it's rolling into.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I believe there's also some things still at the federal government happening around that as well.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Maybe the meeting yesterday helped.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You never know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Also, Chris Gensel is very good.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Sometimes what he tells me, but he does get back to me.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I would have to agree with that assessment.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Councilmember Wilson.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks what hurdles prevent DSS from meeting Intro 101's 15-day response requirement, given processing is just under 25 days. Dalton cites the October Access HRA status portal; French says applications with no back-and-forth are close to 15 days, but many still require returns.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson questions DSS on 15-day application response hurdle

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Just one question regarding Introduction 101, which would require the response in 15 days.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I noticed in your testimony you said that you've gotten it down to just under 25.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So I'm just curious what the hurdles are.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: To meeting the 15 day.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'll start and certainly anyone wants to jump in after that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So there's just a couple of innovations to mention there as we answer.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think we are providing information back to the partners involved in a very regular basis, but I think the important thing that we will be rolling out at the end of October

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: is the client accessibility in the Access HRA app for them to be able to see the current status.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so, you know, as soon as we receive the application, that will get posted, and we'll be able to provide additional details via the app.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I think just having that kind of availability will really change both the feeling about the process as well as might actually improve the process because if we need updates, if there are things

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: that need to be corrected, people will be able to see them more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think also just further, as the Executive Deputy Commissioner said, right, we've just started seeing the impacts of the more integrated streamlined approval process.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we expect that to further, right, hopefully reduce those numbers of days.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I would say the average day that was also very much predicated on how many times an application package needs to go back and forth with the provider.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I would say in instances where there is no back and forth, we are.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Pretty close to that 15 days, but I think while we've seen reduction, we are still seeing a good percentage of packages do need to go back and forth

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: between us and the providers to make sure at least the information we really must have to be able to approve a package to go forward is actually correct in the package.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we're sort of focusing on many different efforts to bring that down as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks for the most common reasons units fail habitability inspections. Dalton lists water temperature failures at about 41%, electrical outlet deficiencies at 33%, missing apartment numbers and window guard violations near 19%, refrigerator temperature failures at 18%, and other issues.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks most common reasons units fail habitability inspections

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What are the most common reasons that units fail habitability inspections?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I'll let the Executive Deputy Commissioner take that one.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I've got it, though.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I need it.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I got you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: You're very welcome.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I've got it right here.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And you can feel free to jump in.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So the top reason, which happens about 40% of the time, are water temperature failures, followed by electric outlet deficiencies, missing apartment numbers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Sorry, hold on, hold on.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you have the...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Corresponding percentages for each.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So 40% are water temp.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: How much for the...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I'll give you the, if it's helpful, I'll give you the closer to exact.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So water temperature failures are about 41%.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Electrical outlet deficiencies are 33%.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: If you'd like me to keep going.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
