utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If you could follow up with us with those, that would be really helpful.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And again, unless I'm incorrect, this is for the HRA inspections, but they seem like pretty common things that would happen in inspections regardless.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Hudson cites a state comptroller report finding DSS approved units with hazardous violations and asks how recordkeeping allowed a new client to move into a unit another client transferred out of. Dalton disputes parts of the report and cites the rental assistance integrity unit as a backstop.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DSS on comptroller report and hazardous unit approvals

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, a recent report by the New York State Comptroller on the administration of the City FEPS program for home-based clients

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: found that DSS had repeatedly approved housing units with hazardous violations, including approving a client to move into an apartment with significant habitability issues despite previously approving another City FEPS client's transfer out of that same apartment

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: due to habitability issues.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you think the procedure envisioned by this bill would help avoid such problems in the future, or are there ways the process outlined in the bill could be improved or tweaked to be more effective?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then if I can also just ask specifically, because I've had a similar constituent case like this where I could not understand how the city would approve someone to live under such horrible conditions, what type of record keeping

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: is being done that somebody in this particular case, somebody new is moving into the same unit that somebody was already moved out of?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think the agency does dispute some of the findings in the controller's report, including that there was somebody to be, there was somebody eventually to be moved into that unit, but was not currently living in that unit.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That said, obviously we care about the safety and habitability of the units that we're inspecting and that we're placing people in.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I think I maintain that we think of the current process that we've been rolling out in the pilot

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: strikes the right balance between providers and HRA, splitting the inspections, the use of

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: virtual in all of the ways that you rightly point out where we can still check, but that we can use those kinds of technologies to make the process faster for smaller repairs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then us, yes, going back out for larger repairs.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think important to note that we've also established within our accountability office a rental assistance integrity unit, and they do reviews of our inspections.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so there is a backstop.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There is additional accountability.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But certainly we would want to hear about the experience of one of your constituents if or that you may have seen yourself a unit that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: You didn't find to be at the level we should be allowing folks to move into.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think those are all very important, and we would want to understand.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: what might have gone wrong in that process.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm happy to share that in greater detail offline, but it was a situation with a mother who had

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: three children, one of whom had special needs, and the conditions were just horrific.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Rats, rodents,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: water leaks, mold, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then the child, you know, essentially couldn't go to school.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: They couldn't shower.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: They stopped going to school because they were unable to shower.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And we couldn't get them out of the apartment fast enough.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You know, it's all the typical, you know, issues that I'm sure so many of us have seen and you all have experienced too, where we can't get the voucher transfer.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We can't get approval for the new unit.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: She had already secured a new apartment, but they couldn't get the payment.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It's just, you know, bureaucracy, right?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But in the meantime, the kids weren't in school, which was a separate problem.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And they had to continue to endure those conditions while they sort of waited for everything to go through.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: That's exactly why we're here today.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how many failing inspections are major versus minor and how many apartments the pilot has covered. French and Reed say specifics will follow, but the pilot allows expedited re-inspection for five or fewer minor defects and has reduced average inspections from 2.2 to 1.7.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about major vs minor inspection failures and pilot re-inspections

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I wanted to just ask, go back to the units that don't pass inspection, the failing inspections.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How many are major issues versus minor issues?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I don't think we have that with us today.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We can get back to you on what we have in our data as to just the breakdown in regards to.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And maybe what we can do is take that list that I read out the percentages of and know whether they're major or minor.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: And how many, you may have mentioned this, and forgive me if you did, but how many apartments have been inspected as part of that pilot program?

utterances.text: I don't know that we have that, but we do about 8,500 a year at HRA, so it's probably, you know, nine-twelfths of that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That would be my, but we can perhaps get that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Nine-twelfths of 8,500.

utterances.text: I'm writing that down.

utterances.text: Has the pilot reduced the number of re-inspections?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think it has, and Andrea, please jump in as well, but I think to be eligible for the pilot, not everything's eligible for the pilot.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I believe it's five or more minor conditions, but I'll let the executive deputy commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Talk a little bit more about those specifics on the re-inspection pilot.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that, Administrator.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So while it has simplified the process in terms of the provider will work with the landlord to remediate the issues and then send us photos and videos to show that it's corrected, many of the failures that we see are minor.

utterances.text: So many of the items that Commissioner shared are minor inspections, like the water temperature, refrigerator temperature, and the clogged sinks.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Those are all minor repairs.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: They're quick turnaround when the landlord is able to remediate quickly.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are your definitions of minor versus major aligned with DOB and HPD?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Our apartment review checklist is aligned with DOB and HPD.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, just confirming.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We partnered to prepare.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then with the pilot, you've shared a lot of the learnings.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are there any challenges that have emerged?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I don't know that there's challenges that we would say.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I mean, I do.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think what's good is that we have found it to actually be useful and helpful, which was our hope, which is why we're very much looking forward to expanding it right across the system in the first part of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I think, you know, with everything you learn along the way, but I think ultimately we see this as very positive and beneficial to everyone, especially speeding along, right, re-inspections that really just need to address a few minor issues.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I don't want to misspeak, but I think we have seen at least a slight reduction, which may be more than slight, from about 2.2 inspections per to 1.7.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think unless that's, unless that I've got that wrong.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, so that, I mean, so we've also seen some improvement there as well.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about challenges with landlords who do not make repairs and whether there is a process to stop using repeat offenders. French says there is no formal removal process yet, but DSS is looking at assessment and escalation, including for fraud and criminality.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about challenges with landlords and repeat offenders

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then, you know, we've already mentioned sort of some of the anecdotes with the challenges that we've heard about directly from constituents

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: and also difficult landlords, you know, who are not making repairs.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What are some of the challenges that DSS faces in working with landlords, especially when it comes to ensuring that tenants are living in safe conditions?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I mean, I think we, you know, we make it very clear, and I think through our really structured inspection process, that we expect a level of professionalism and care from our landlords, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And that anyone, you know, moving out with a city FEPS voucher should, you know, have the same care and treatment and responsiveness to their apartment as any other New Yorker.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And so, you know, during that process where we're doing the inspections, we obviously have more sort of leverage and oversight with the landlords in regards to, right, approval of the unit to be utilized in the program.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We do also, when individuals are leaving shelter, right, really let them know also what their rights are once they move out, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Once you're a permanent resident, we don't.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Have as much of insight necessarily into the relationship with the landlord, but we make sure that everyone understands that, you know, what your rights are and how you can report issues where landlords are not being responsive

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: to you in regards to conditions and other things that should be addressed in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you have any sort of formal process for, or let's call it an exit ramp for landlords that have a history of

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: refusal to do repairs or any of these complaints, consistent, you know, major failures?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Major issues that are causing them to fail inspections and so forth.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is there a formal process for removing those landlords?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So there isn't, I don't want to misspeak necessarily, there isn't a removal process that is currently in place of that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: There are some things we're looking at internally around, I think, assessment process for landlords who come to us with new units who we may have had issues in the past.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We can follow up on.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I don't want to misspeak right here in regards to that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Maybe removal isn't the most accurate way to express this.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But essentially, is there a process when you know that somebody is a repeat offender?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You know, for not renting more units from them or continuing to rent those units?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Where, yeah, we're currently looking at what would be a process that sort of aligns within, you know, allowability of identifying landlords who have potentially had

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: problematic units in the past or challenges engaging with the program and following the appropriate rules and expectations.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We can follow up with some more details.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then, I mean, this is just coming to me, so forgive me.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But do you know of...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Any folks in the program that are on the worst landlords list?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I just, I can't, I don't want to speak specifically.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I would want to check.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You look like you have an answer.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: No, I don't have an answer to the problematic landlords, but we are working on a landlord elevation escalation list, but it's not related to landlords that are...

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: That poor character, it's around criminality and fraud.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so we don't yet have a process for the bad landlords.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So it's administrator mentioned, we'll get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Councilmember Brewer is suggesting the use of AI to complete that process for you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about median lease-up time from shopping letter to move-in. Dalton provides averages: 244 days in 2024, 221 in 2025, and 236 year-to-date in 2026, and notes application processing is about 21 days in community and 31 days in shelter.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about lease-up times for CityFHEPS vouchers

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Regarding Intro 100 in relation to requiring reporting of lease-up times for housing vouchers, what is the median time it takes for an applicant to lease up for the first time from shopping letter issuance to move in?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I think those are...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't have medium, but I do have average or mean.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I can give it to you for the last couple of years.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So starting with 2024, the average days was 244.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: For 2025, the average days was 221.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then year to date, it's 236 for 2026.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Year to date, 236.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So that's not...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Necessarily looking great, at least in comparing directly to 2025.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is there a difference in the time it takes applicants to lease up based on whether they apply while living in community versus residing in shelter?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So when we think about that data, I'm going to go back to the time of application to processing on the city FEP side.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So you're not going to hear numbers in the hundreds here.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: You're going to hear.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So for in community, it's about 21 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And for folks in shelter, it's 31 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And then that's that average of around 28 where we're doing better in the last couple of months with 24.8.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So those are the numbers that fit together there.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And it stands to reason that folks who are in community already have a unit established, and so they're often applying for CityFAP's voucher to stay in that unit, and so the timing is faster.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what DSS is doing to close the lease-up gap and how CityFHEPS compares with one-time assistance. French says CityFHEPS is a voucher while SOTA is not, and recertification has about 90% retention with a four-month renewal window.
chapters.title: DSS explains steps to address lease-up gap and SOTA differences

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are there any specific steps you're taking to address the gap?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think all of the steps we have already mentioned in terms of reorganization and attempting to process as fast as possible the inspections that we just discussed and so on.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think we are very focused on doing that as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And is there a difference between folks?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Leasing up with a city FEPS voucher versus a one-time assistance voucher.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: You referred to soda?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Right, the SOTA program.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Yeah, I think first, and I'll let the executive director, Christopher, speak as well.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: CityFaps is a voucher.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Soda would not be a voucher.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Soda is a sort of one-year...

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Commitment based upon certain criteria that individuals meet.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Many of those people are not eligible for city FEPS because they have employment, they have income.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And so we track them differently.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we don't really have comparable timing between those two pieces.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Also, when it comes to soda, individuals, when they sort of step forward for soda, they have identified the unit most likely.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what is the median time it takes applicants who are recertifying their eligibility to lease up?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So as it comes to recertification,

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: That happens very differently than lease up.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So those are also not really comparable for someone who's recertifying four months before the end of that sort of lease period.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We will start to send individuals reminders that they can actually renew their.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: CityFEP's voucher now.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So individuals have a four-month period, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So basically from month eight to 12, at any point, someone can step forward and say, and submit the documentation that's needed to do a lease up.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think, you know, we see about 90% of, you know, retention rates.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Year over year.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I think that sort of gives a sense on like how things are going.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we don't expect that to be a hundred as people will move.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: People, you know, may pass away.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: There are many other reasons of that, but I would say that that I think gives an indicator on the recertification process in general.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we just, we allow a longer period of time where people can choose to start that process.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks whether Intro 100 reporting would capture delays from the reinstated rent reasonableness policy. French says the reporting would cover shopping letter to move-out, acknowledges the policy added delays, and says rent-regulated unit reviews will shift to after move-in to mitigate impact.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about rent reasonableness policy impact on lease-up

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And the reinstated rent reasonableness policy has increased the time between pre-clearance and lease-up.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: To your understanding, if this legislation was enacted, would that increase in time be captured?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we...

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We have, I mean, any period of time from, as the legislation has it, right, it's from when the shopping letter and someone is initially deemed eligible to when they move out.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So that would include all aspects of that process, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Both the period of time it finds to find a unit, identify it, the inspection process, and then the package process.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I will say as it relates to rent review and rent reasonableness, right, we did roll that out in the late spring with very good intentions of we do want to ensure, right, the city is not being.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Charged rents that are outside of allowable rents, whether it's rent regulated rent or market rate comparables.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We did understand and see an unanticipated impact of rolling that out, especially as it relates to the rent regulated aspect and the engagement with HCR on legal rents that it did add to the

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: pre-clearance and clearance process.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Just last week, we sent a communication out to the community that

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: That part of the process for all rent regulated units will now be shifted to after move in

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: as we have a process where we can still identify if someone has incorrectly charged a rent where the city can collect the overpayments while not impacting someone's ability to move in.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we should see that impact mitigate.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Down shortly.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We obviously have to get through some of the cases that have built up, but we think that that is a very positive shift that I have heard people in the community are very happy with.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about time from shopping letter to initial submission and processing times for shelter versus community applicants. DSS lacks some data but reports 28 days average overall, 31 days for shelter, and 21 days for community, and will assess further disaggregation.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions DSS on Intro 101 application response times

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to intro number 101.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: In relation to CityFEP's application response times.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For people experiencing homelessness, what is the average length of time from issuance of a CityFEP's shopping letter to initial submission of a CityFEP's packet to DHS HRA?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We do not have that information available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: At the moment, but could you follow up with it?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I've talked to our data people.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I don't want to promise as to the level of effort that would take, but we can see.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think also we just would want to sort of understand that within that time frame, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: There's much that could actually...

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Leads to that level of time for someone based upon EA, there aren't available apartments just for the general reason, or if someone has specifically like the commissioner mentioned, as well as some other things.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But we can see if that is something that is able to be run.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, and if it is able to be run, could you please include, can you disaggregate it by DHS versus HRA DV shelters, as well as the average number of days it takes for HRA to review an application after it's submitted?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We can look at that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm just putting it all out there.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not the data expert.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But yes, we will assess all of those requests.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And we will obviously follow up with you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is the average length of time to process and approve a CityFEPS application from initial submission to check issuance?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think we've provided that data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That's the same number, the 28 days, if I understand your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And again, we're doing better in the most recent months.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Slightly different for in community.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And do you have that disaggregated?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: By applications from shelter versus in community?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I'll run through it.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think, and again, folks can tell me if I get this wrong, but from application to outcome on average over calendar year 2026, that's 28 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: If you're in shelter, it's 31.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So a portion of those folks are in shelter and it's 31 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And if you're in community, it's 21 days.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, those same numbers then.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then could you further disaggregate by average length of time from initial packet submission to final approval of the application?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Or the average length of time from final approval to move-in date?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the first one is the answer I just gave.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So initial submission to approval.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we do not have with us the approval to move in date.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And I don't know if we capture that data, but we could certainly follow up.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what causes package rejections. French says outright denials are rare and most issues are returns for corrections, often due to document errors or income ineligibility, and says DSS can look at publishing return reasons.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about common reasons for CityFHEPS package returns

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what are the most common reasons for rejections of CityFEP's packages?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I mean, I'll let the executive deputy commissioner weigh in there as well.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think it's more of returns versus outright rejections necessarily, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: There may be people who ultimately are not eligible for city FEPS at that point.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So that would, in theory, be a rejection.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But I think much of it is really more about what are the causes for returns, which the executive deputy commissioner team have also done.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I'll boast for her.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Great work to really start to turn the tide on the amount of returns that are going on with our providers.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Just for you.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: As Administrator mentioned, it's very rare that we see denial at the point where applications are submitted.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's the return that's delayed.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: For an application to be denied, it's because someone is employed and now they're over income or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Very rare does it get to the point where it comes to us and get denied.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Once it's submitted, it's because you're eligible and it's just making sure the documents are correct.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, do you think it's possible to publish the most common reason that we see denial at the point where applications are submitted?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: for rejections each year to improve overall submission accuracy.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We can look for that.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's the return that's delayed.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And I mean, it's really tiny.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: But yeah.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: For an application to be denied,

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think just for clarity, though, are you, is it rejections you're looking for or is it return reasons that you're looking for?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's because someone is employed and now they're over income or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Very rare does it get to the point where it comes to us and get denied.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Well, return reasons.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If that's where the rejections are.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Once it's submitted, it's because you're eligible and it's just making sure the documents are correct.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Well, ineligibility.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, do you think it's possible to publish the most common reason?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Okay, ineligibility.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: All right, so we can look at that, yes.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what percentage of applications are returned for correction and whether documents go stale during review. DSS says it will follow up on percentages and explains document validity was extended from four to six months and is frozen at application submission.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about returned applications and stale documents

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What percentage of city FEPS applications are returned for correction?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I don't have that with me.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Okay, I think we can get, I want to make sure we have the right data point for you so we can get back to you with the percentage that are returned for correction.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, and then sort of in the same vein, what percentage of packages are returned to providers because the documents, i.e.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Leases or pay stubs, grew stale or outdated while awaiting HRA review?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we'll look into, I will say, I'm not sure how much we can sort of disaggregate by percentage-wise based on specific reason.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I know we have gotten sort of much more specific around that moving forward, so there might be something that we can provide now and then potentially more detail in the future.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But we have spent a lot of effort working with the providers, right, on sort of identifying to them.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we can provide that to you of like, these are the main reasons why packages are being returned.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think also through the streamlining, right, we're looking at the whole of package, which has allowed us, I think, to hone in on.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: These are the real reasons.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: These are the primary reasons from an eligibility perspective that we will return this to you versus some other things we may now, based on that approach, determine that is not something that needs to be returned for the package to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: When does a lease or pay stub become outdated?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I shared that we have now increased the time of the life of documents, and so six months, and because of the six months.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Also, when the application...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So, sorry, the increased time is now six months?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What was it before?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: From four months to six months.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And also, at the point that the application is first submitted...

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We freeze the time frame so the documents do not go stale.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: You freeze the time frame at the point of submission.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So you no longer have to update the documents.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Or resubmit, effectively.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Resubmit, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what steps DSS takes before informing applicants of approval, denial, or needed corrections. Reed explains biweekly case manager contact and an October Access HRA portal update that will show real-time application status and client dependencies.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about application review steps and client portal updates

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What steps does DSS take upon receiving an application for CityFEPS before letting the applicant know if the application has been approved, denied, or requires correction or additional information?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So are you informing somebody immediately?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Like, at what point are they finding out after that six-month period that their application needs correction?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Just a point of clarity.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So a shopping letter is issued to a client.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's good for six months.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's automatically updated unless something else happens and they're no longer potentially eligible.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So that's automatically done.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: At the point that the application is submitted, the client is in constant communication with their case manager or housing specialist on a biweekly basis.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: As we shared earlier also that going forward this October, we will be updating the client portal so that clients can now see real-time status of their application.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So they'll see when it's submitted.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: They'll see if it's returned and whether there are any client dependencies that they need to take action on.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Or whether it's something that the provider needs to do, and then at the point that it's being reviewed and approved and ready for checks.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And if I could add, I do think that's a very significant innovation and an important aspect of transparency for the whole process.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think it will help put a lot of folks'minds at ease.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: They'll be able to check it whenever they want.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And as the Executive Deputy Commissioner said, know if they have additional items they have to follow up on, know that we got it, know the exact...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think it will go a long way.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And even not just transparency, but speeding the process so people can take action more quickly.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I think it's important and would love everyone's help to get the word out that that will be available.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We'll do our part as well.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I think it's a game changer.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how shopping letters are renewed after six months and whether the six-month duration is necessary. Reed says letters are automatically renewed if eligibility continues; French says the six-month checkpoint reconfirms income and baseline eligibility.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson questions shopping letter renewal and six-month eligibility

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But with regards to the shopping letter, you said they are...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Automatically renewed after six months?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: They're automated.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: They're automated, so it's an electronic process.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So it's issued.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's available in Access HRA, so the client can go and see in their portal, the shopping letter, the case manager and or housing specialist provide a copy, and so that...

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's automatically renewed as long as they continue their eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you know the average time it takes for someone to find an available unit?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: that we don't have that average time, just given there's a variety of different factors.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think we're going to look at the data that we do have to sort of see what might be something we could track as to like when the CityFAPS right package is submitted.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: That is probably the best sort of one of the markers that we have at the moment to look at.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so I guess I'm trying to figure out.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How do you determine that six months is the most appropriate time for the eligibility?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think the six months is based upon what we think is an appropriate time to just reconfirm income eligibility in case there have been changes in income, given that it's really done on the back end.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So it's not something that the individual in shelter needs to take action on.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: It's just it's a good checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So in case something has changed.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We would then address it at that point.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And if the person is no longer eligible, we wouldn't want to renew that letter.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we would want the shelter provider to also understand you need to engage this household around a different plan for housing stability and what might their pathway be.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So that's what bases on the six month.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: It's really about just trying to confirm the income and those other baseline eligibilities have remained the same.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: How many people are deemed ineligible?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: after the six months based on that?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I would need to get back to you on that data point.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I'd need to talk to our data folks on that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, just...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I understand where you're going.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand what you're trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I think the data you've already requested, which we do have, will tell you that time frame.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So from shopping letter to process to application submission, we'll give you that first data point.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I haven't looked at the data.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's going to be longer than six months.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I understand the secondary question about, is that a meaningful?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I'm just I'm just thinking and I don't know the answer, to be clear, but I'm just thinking, you know, if somebody is eligible for a city FEPS voucher.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Six months from that point, they're probably still eligible.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: They're more likely to be eligible than not, let's say, to still be eligible.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so I'm just trying to figure out why we have the six-month duration on that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And is that, and again, I don't know the answer, and I know that you may not know it in this moment, but something to consider is then, is that six-month...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Duration or expiration necessary.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And maybe there's another opportunity for streamlining the process that allows that shopping letter to be eligible a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And we've already testified that it is very rare that people are found ineligible.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: It's only returns, really.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We've already testified to that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So I understand.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then people have to go through the same hassle of, you know, all of that after the six months.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But I'm glad you're with me on that one.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how long DSS takes to reprocess corrected applications and whether Q-Rent lacks core functionality for shelter housing coordinators. French says reprocessing data will be checked; Reed says the current system allows multiple search points and robust application submission.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about reprocessing time and Q-Rent functionality

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: If an application requires corrections or additional information and the applicant provides the requested updates, what is the median time it takes DSS to reprocess the application?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We would have to get back to you on if we have that data point that can be pulled.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the next question just to ask it, but I feel like we've sort of addressed it.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But if you have anything additional to add, do let me know.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What efforts are underway to help decrease package processing times?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: The software for processing packages, Q-Rent, lacks core functionality for shelter housing coordinators.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For instance, they cannot search for clients by name, only their WMS case number, and there's no client dashboard.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are you aware of these limitations?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: The current application system, you are able to search by client information and WMS ID, current ID.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: There's a number of search points, address and landlord information.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, so that our information is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So the...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Some of these challenges with core functionality have perhaps already been addressed.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is that safe to say?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: In terms of the application submission, the functionality are pretty robust.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Hudson says the committee will move on to Intro 641 and checks whether colleagues have additional questions. She recognizes Council Member Brewer.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson moves to Intro 641 and recognizes Council Member Brewer

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And then moving on to intro number 641.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And before I do move on, I just want to check in with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Are there any additional questions from folks?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Yeah, Councilmember Brewer.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how often shopping letters expire and whether constituent panic reflects a small or large problem. Scott French says the six-month letter is automatically renewed if eligibility continues and DSS wants to understand cases where constituents experience problems.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about shopping letter expiration and voucher panic

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You've discussed this a lot, and maybe you said it, but the six-month, the expiration of the voucher.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How often does that happen?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is it just my imagination that people come to our office because it's such a panic moment?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But maybe it's a very small number of people who actually have that experience.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We have a lot of clients who come in with that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I just wanted to understand that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And I think we would love further details from you to understand what might be driving that for them.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So the sixth month is for the shopping letter, right?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So it's the sort of presumptive eligibility.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And for, you know, that is automatically renewed as we do sort of back end.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Data tracking to ensure the information looks the same, you're still income eligible, and that letter should be provided to the household.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So if there's confusion or concerns about that that are happening, we would definitely want to talk to you about that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But as the commissioner said, we'll...

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Who's the commissioner?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Often is what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And it's very fixable.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: It should not, and it is fixable.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So we would want that brought to our attention.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we'll, as we said, look at if there is a longer period of time than six months that it can be expanded to as well.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks whether DSS is finding new owners willing to rent to voucher holders or relying on the same landlords. French says DSS is always trying to expand the landlord universe and can follow up with data on new participating owners.
chapters.title: Brewer asks whether new landlords are participating in CityFHEPS

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are you finding that there are more owners?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I just wanted to add that we rolled out the six-month time frame in May, so we will just be coming up on the first sort of six-month cycle, so we should see it.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It should not be so bumpy.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Are there new owners that you're finding that are willing to rent, or you still have to go back to the same?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: persons, although you have new buildings, I understand that, but there aren't that many new buildings for the incomes that you're looking for, if I may suggest that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But are there new, you know, private owners that have buildings that are offering their apartments?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or is it same old?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think we're always open to new coming in, and I think we do see new.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We could get back to you on what we're sort of seeing in the data.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I don't know, Andrea, if there's anything there, but it's not just the same old, and we are definitely always trying to expand the universe of landlords to partner with us.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether landlords can receive only part of the total subsidy at the beginning of the month because the state pays shelter allowance in two installments. Dalton confirms this and Reed explains the landlord portal shows subsidy and shelter allowance portions, with a possible missed-payment distinction to be confirmed.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano questions DSS on split rental subsidy payments

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Councilor Vermarano.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, you say that DSS issues its portion of rental payments on the 26th and that landlords...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: enrolled in electronic payments receive the money within 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But you also explained that the state's shelter allowance is paid in two installments at the beginning and middle of the month.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So even when the city does everything correctly, is it possible for a landlord to receive only part of the total rental subsidy at the beginning of the month?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: We can control the piece that we can control, and we pay, as you said, on the 26th for the upcoming month.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But, right, the state pays in two tranches for people who are receiving that shelter allowance.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so, in fact, of course, the landlord could receive up to four payments, one from us, two from the state, and then the tenant portion.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Does DSS provide landlords with a payment calendar showing exactly how much is coming from the city, how much is coming from the state, and when each payment should arrive?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I know we, and I'll defer, but I know we are clear at the beginning and request, require the landlord to sign off on the payment process.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But I'll defer to see if there's any additional communication about a schedule.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So at the approval point in the process, the landlord do get an approval notice that shows the payment amount.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Certainly over time that may change.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so we are looking to update the system so that we would send out additional notices.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We're not quite there yet.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: It's one of the enhancements.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: But as I shared earlier.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: In the landlord portal, you're now able to see the government portion.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So you can see the subsidy amount and you can see the shelter allowance amount.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So then the only other portion is the client direct share.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I guess I'm wondering, does the landlord portal currently distinguish between an actual missed payment and a payment that hasn't arrived yet because of the state's schedule?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I'm not sure the status.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We'll have to confirm the language as to what's listed there.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: It definitely shows the payments made.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it would indicate a, say, missed payment from the state WMS system, but we can get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Would you support making that distinction visible to every participating landlord if it's not, Peretti?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Yeah, not that I get to ask the questions here, but to ask my colleagues a clarifying question, and maybe it's clear because the amounts are different anyway, but when we say the government portion, does it indicate the city portion versus the state portion?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yes, it does say the subsidy portion.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: There's a code, I think it's SE, and it says subsidy portion, and then you'll see the shelter allowance portion.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So it would seem to be that we're transparent about that now and that it would be clear.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: if there was, in fact, a missed payment from the system.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether DSS tracks additional shelter nights caused by administrative delays and how many households have an identified apartment but await final approval. French says DSS does not have that data now and will look into it, including possible shelter cost estimates.
chapters.title: Morano asks if DSS tracks shelter nights due to administrative delays

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's say there's a family in a shelter that has found an apartment, and the landlord is ready, the family's ready, but the application is sitting somewhere in the city's approval process.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Is DSS tracking how many additional nights?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: People spend in shelters specifically because of administrative delays?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We do not have that data available at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We will look at our systems to see, but that is not a data point I have today.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And just to, I'm sorry, just to add there, and again, my colleagues can correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: But the...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: That process is the process we've been talking about that's ranging from around 24 days to 28 days.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so it's a small piece, at least to my understanding, of the overall process.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: And so I think we certainly can know if there are...

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: What we're giving you are averages, right?

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There will be cases where it goes above that.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I don't know that we would consider that an administrative challenge.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: There are back and forth that need to happen in order for us to process appropriately.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If we don't know how long, perhaps we know how many, can you tell us how many households currently have an identified apartment but are waiting for final city approval?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We don't have that with us today, but we can look at the data and get back to you with what we have.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: When you do get that, if you could also include some sort of estimate or calculation about the additional shelter expenditures that taxpayers are footing the bill for associated with that waiting period.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We'll look into that and see what can be estimated there.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks about median time between correction notification and apartment registration, and the breakdown of corporate, professional, small, and owner-occupant landlords. French says DSS does not capture those details and will follow up.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about landlord correction timelines and landlord types

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Among landlords who are required to make a correction,

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What is the median time between notification of the correction and successful apartment registration?

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And we don't capture that information in the system, right?

utterances.text: So that's not something we can provide, I think.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Among landlords currently participating in the City FIPS program, how many are corporate landlords, professional property management companies, small to mid-sized private landlords, so owning just two to ten buildings, and individual owner-occupants?

utterances.text: We'll have to get back to you with that information.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We don't have breakdowns with us today.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It would be great to know, too, how your interactions may differ with different types of landlords.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For example, you know, an individual owner, occupant, somebody who owns, let's say, a private, you know, two-family home or something like that versus...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: corporation, and if the challenges are the same.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks what support is available to landlords who speak languages other than English. Reed says providers have bilingual staff and interpretation contracts, but Dalton confirms landlord forms are only in English while client-facing forms are available in many languages.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks about language access for landlords

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: What support is available to landlords who speak a primary language other than English?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So at the point in time where the landlord is working with the provider, many providers have bilingual staff.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: In addition to that, they have language services contracts and interpretation services.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: That's available across the agency also.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Okay, so do you know which languages the forms are available in?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: I've got that here.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: So landlord forms are available.

utterances.speaker: Erin Dalton
utterances.text: Landlord forms are only available in English, but client-facing forms are available in English, Spanish, Arabic, Urdu, Bengali, French, Haitian, Creole, Korean, Polish, Albanian, Yiddish, traditional Chinese, simplified Chinese, Italian, and Russian.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Is there a reason you believe that materials are not available to landlords in all of the same languages?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: I think it's a good point and something we can look at.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.title: DSS describes landlord complaint process and pain points

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And how do landlords currently submit complaints regarding administrative issues with rental assistance payments?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So currently, landlords are able to submit their complaints through the landlord portal.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And just hot off the press, we now have on the DSS website just about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Heard it here first at the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: There's a web-based form, and so there's a link that directly sends that to part of the reorg.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: We have the stakeholders outreach and engagement team that is specifically developed to support landlords around this issue.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And so now they're able to submit their increase to us that way.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And what are the common pain points you hear from landlords who participate in rental subsidy programs?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And I will be glad to share some of those I've heard directly from landlords.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: I want to say that, you know, when you think about the housing journey, there are different touch points.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So certainly at the front end, landlord, all of what you talked about, timeliness.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: and transparency.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: And then on the back end, it's about the payments, which we have shared the dependencies on the various payment types.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Reed
utterances.text: So those are usually the concerns that we get.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: And I'll say the tech enhancements that we're doing on the systems we've talked about today, many of them are directly in response to issues we've heard from the landlords to increase transparency, access to information, and understanding where is something in the process.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: So I think when we follow up with, right, what are those enhancements and when are we going to see them, that will probably give you an additional insight into.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: What we're trying to do to sort of expand and improve that type of communication and understanding of what's happening.

chapters.summary: Hudson shares a constituent landlord story in which a brownstone owner exited the CityFHEPS program because inspections and administrative issues were too difficult, yet rented to the tenant outside the program. She says better systems could help more people secure safe housing.
chapters.title: Chair Hudson shares landlord anecdote about failed voucher process

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I do want to just share one quick anecdote and I'd have to get the specific details to you offline, but we had

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: a landlord who owned a brownstone in the district and was trying to rent to someone with a voucher.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And it was just an impossible process for him.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: They couldn't get somebody out to do the inspection, to verify certain things.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: She was having some issues.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And ultimately, and I wish we had more folks like this, he just rented it to her at the rate that he would have been, that she would have, whatever the total amount would have been

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: outside of the program because she was just so desperate.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And he wanted to be able to provide the unit to somebody in need.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so he, you know, went without the, he formally exited the program and just said, this is just been too difficult.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It's too much, you know, but I want to keep her as a tenant or have her as a tenant.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so, you know, obviously that's.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: An anomaly and we don't usually see people like that.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But just to share that, you know, there are probably so many more people who would be in safe and secure housing if some of these systems actually worked better, you know, for them.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And if only we could have every landlord like this gentleman who was willing to take on this tenant no matter what, you know, unfortunately we don't.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so, you know, I think the...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: A lot of, and I know you all share the end goals and a lot of these concerns, and I know we're all working towards the same thing, but these are the types of things I think, you know, what Councilmember Brewer was saying.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: We get the folks, whether they're tenants or landlords who've just had, you know, impossible experiences trying to do the right thing and just trying to get housed or provide housing

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: that we as government have just made it so incredibly difficult for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: So just wanted to.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: To share that.

chapters.title: Chair Hudson asks for list of landlords in CityFHEPS program

utterances.text: At the risk of, I'm just going to ask for this on the record.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I was debating whether or not I should ask on the record, but I'm just going to ask.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: But is it possible to get a list of landlords that are receiving, that are in the CityFEP's program?

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: We'll get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: But yes, we will speak with our general counsel and get back to you on what is able to be provided.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

chapters.title: Chair Hudson thanks DSS and closes agency testimony

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson

utterances.speaker: Scott French
utterances.text: Thank you.
