chapters.summary: Brandon Lloyd of URI says his organization provides shelter to 4,000 people nightly and supports Intros 101 and 641. He says administrative delays prolong shelter stays and late subsidy payments can lead to arrears and loss of housing for domestic violence survivors and others.
chapters.title: Brandon Lloyd of URI testifies in support of Intros 101 and 641

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: My name is Brandon Lloyd, and I'm the Director of Government Affairs here at URI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: URI is the largest provider of domestic violence shelter services in the country and a leading provider of transitional housing for families experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: Each night, URI provides safe, temporary housing to 4,000 individuals across 28 locations here in New York City and across four boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: And through trauma-informed and client-centered services, we work to disrupt cycles of violence and homelessness for survivors, youth, and communities all over New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: I want to especially thank Chair Hudson for your continued leadership and partnership on behalf of our residents in your district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: URI is proud to operate shelters in your community, and we deeply appreciate your ongoing support for both the families and pets that we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: We would also like to thank Council Members Brewer and Ressler for their leadership and the members of the committee for helping New Yorkers maintain stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: URI strongly supports Intro 101 and 641, as together these bills would extremely streamline City FEPS application response times

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: and increase transparency within the administration of City FEPS by establishing clear expectations for timely application responses and recurring rental payments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: As these improvements are essential to ensuring that eligible households experiencing are at risk of homelessness, including families and individuals living in both DHS and HRA shelters, such as

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: Domestic violence shelters can use these vouchers to secure safe and maintain stable and affordable permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: For the families that we serve here at URI, access to safe and affordable housing is essential to leading independent lives free from violence and crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: City FEPS is a crucial lifeline for families and individuals transitioning from temporary housing to permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: However, access to vouchers alone does not guarantee that a family can secure and maintain permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: As many of you know, administrative delays unnecessarily prolong shelter stays when families are ready to move, and late subsidy payments can lead to increased rental arrears, disputes with property owners, and the fear of losing permanent housing placement that took months to secure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: These delays can carry serious consequences for all households that rely on city FEPS, including families and individuals in shelter and those at risk of homelessness,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: losing an apartment opportunity, extending a shelter stay, or facing pressure to return to a harmful environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: In conclusion, URI applauds the Council's efforts to make this process more responsive and trauma-informed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: Intro 101 and 641 take meaningful steps in addressing administrative delays by keeping these households informed while they seek housing and delivering rental assistance on a dependable schedule once they are housed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: We respectfully urge the Council to pass Intros 101 and 641 and to work with the Department of Social Services to ensure clear communication support systems capable

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: of meeting these deadlines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing our partnership with the council and to help families secure permanent housing and remain there safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brandon Lloyd
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Jerry Hippolyte of Housing Solutions of New York says his organization serves over 7,800 New Yorkers yearly and supports Intros 98, 100, 101, and 641. He says success should be measured by keys to a home, not just a voucher in hand, and urges measuring the entire process from application to move.
chapters.title: Jerry Hippolyte of Housing Solutions of New York testifies on CityFHEPS journey

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Hudson and members of the Committee on General Welfare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: My name is Jerry Hippolyte, Chief of Staff and Head of Government Affairs at Housing Solutions of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: Across more than 30 sites, including 187 supportive housing units, HSNY serves over 7,800 New Yorkers each year and helps over 1,000 into permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: From that experience, we know that CityFEPS is one of the city's most important tools for moving New Yorkers out of shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: But issuing a voucher is not the finish line.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: The real measure of success really speaks to vouchers that go through door to permanent housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: And so that's why HSNY supports the goals of Intros 98, 100, 101, and 641, to which you'll see the full details of our support in the written statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: But together, these bills address critical points in the journey, from timeliness to practical determinations, greater transparency around lease-up times, faster application decisions, and reliable rental assistance payments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: So for individuals experiencing homelessness, every unnecessary delay means more time in a shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: For landlords, delay really undermined the confidence in the program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: And for providers, not to belabor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: but I've heard it from many of my peers, this means losing out on an apartment that we worked really, really hard to secure for one of our clients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: And so we truly encourage the city to measure its city FEPS from application truly to move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: And I'll even add one of the statements that our peers mentioned earlier, even the pre-screening, we're looking at the entire process with this focus on speed, transparency, and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: One of the exciting things that I heard was the live dashboard straight off the press.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: I would love to see what that assessment period actually looks like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: Last but not least, ultimately, success is not a voucher in someone's hand, but the keys to their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jerry Hyppolite
utterances.text: And for that, I say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Yvonne Peña of the Community Service Society presents a survey of 727 CityFHEPS applicants and renewers. She says 93% valued the program but more than half had to resubmit documents, 76% experienced source-of-income discrimination, and 25% had rental assistance stop, often leading to arrears and eviction.
chapters.title: Yvonne Peña of Community Service Society presents survey findings on CityFHEPS

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hudson, for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: My name is Yvonne Pena, and I'm a policy analyst at the Community Service Society of New York, or CSS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: We are a nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Earlier this year, CSS surveyed 727 New Yorkers who had applied for or renewed city FEPS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Of these, 550 had been determined eligible and 497 were currently housed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: We asked about their experiences applying for and maintaining city FEPS, searching for housing, and resolving problems with their subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Our findings speak directly to several issues the committee is considering today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: First, we want to emphasize that CityFEPS is highly valued by recipients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: 93% said the program was worth the effort required to apply for and maintain it, and more than one quarter said they would change nothing or offered positive feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: While most said the instructions of the paperwork were clear and knew which documents to submit, respondents still experienced delays and unnecessary hurdles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: More than half had to submit the same documents more than once, and 44% said the process took a long time to complete.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: A respondent said, the waiting period is very long and stressful, and it's hard to get updates on where my application stands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Having a CityFEP shopping letter does not mean quickly securing housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: More than half of our respondents had trouble finding an apartment within CityFEP's rent limits, and more than one-third spent $1,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: five months or longer searching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: 76% experienced some form of source of income discrimination, which contributed to shopping letters expiring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: One respondent said, finding a place that accepts the program is nearly impossible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Finally, payment interruptions can risk housing stability,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: 25% of respondents said their rental assistance stopped at some point in the previous three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: And of those, 83% accumulated rent arrears, 65% were taken to housing court, and 56% reported being evicted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: One respondent told us, I'm having a problem with CityFest paying my rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: I just moved in not that long ago, but they're not sending payments on time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: I don't want to lose my place that I just got.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: While our research does not tell us what every legislative or administrative solution should look like, it does show the importance of timely decisions,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: understanding how long it takes to find housing, and having systems for tenants, landlords, and DSS to identify and resolve payment problems before they threaten stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Yvonne Peña
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Alec Vanderbilt says he has been trying to get a CityFHEPS voucher for over nine months and found Homebase staff unfamiliar with required documents. He says HRA helped but he is still waiting, and describes dangerous conditions in his building.
chapters.title: Alec Vanderbilt testifies on nine-month wait and Homebase confusion

utterances.text: Hello, my name is Alec Vanderbilt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: I've been nine months and three weeks trying to get the City Phelps voucher, but it started with the tenant situation, so I went to Homebase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: And I took Homebase, everything they require, you know, your HPD form saying you're in danger in the building that you live in, everything that they required.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: And the staff that came to me and everyone was super kind, but none of them even knew what the documents were.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: And they were like, well, you got to bring this, you got to bring this, you got to bring this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: I said, this is all, this is it right here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: And they still didn't comprehend the documentation that was put before them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: So I went back to HRA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: They took care of the situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: like educated me more and we've been there like two years and they helped me like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: reach my voice out and I've been in on outreach doing a lot of outreach everywhere the point is that nothing's coming out of this like home base is like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: Garbage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: It shouldn't even exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: We shouldn't even be working with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: The committees are all doing all that they can to help everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: Even the city is doing the best they can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: Thanks to his aid and help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: And the city of Albs voucher is needed.

utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alec Vanderbilt
utterances.text: That's why I'm still trying to get it.

utterances.text: That's basically all I have to say.

utterances.text: Thank you for sharing that.

chapters.summary: Jorge Jimenez, a former city council worker who is now homeless, describes a concussion, lost savings, street homelessness, and losing eight apartment units. He supports Intro 101 but says the council must also address what happens before and after the voucher process.
chapters.title: Jorge Jimenez testifies on homelessness, lost voucher, and need for reform

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jorge Jimenez
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Jorge Jimenez.

chapters.summary: Pepper Pavlish of Homeless Services United says the coalition represents more than 55 providers and supports Intros 98, 100, 101, 641, and T2026-1424. She calls for effective implementation to make CityFHEPS clearer, more transparent, and more efficient.
chapters.title: Pepper Pavlish of Homeless Services United testifies in support of all five bills

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: My name is Pepper Pavlish, and I'm the Director of Communication and Member Support at Homeless Services United.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: HSU is a coalition representing more than 55 mission-driven homeless service providers throughout New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: We thank the New York City Council for considering these important improvements to the City FEPS program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: As a coalition representing providers across the five boroughs, we know firsthand about the challenges faced by organizations on the ground and the clients we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: As it currently stands, CityFEP is riddled with delays, disruptions, and bureaucratic hurdles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: That impede the process of applying for and assessing housing for tens and thousands of eligible recipients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: We support the five pieces of legislation being discussed today, Intro 98, Intro 100, Intro 101, Intro 641, and T20.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: And we are resolute in our assessment that effective implementation by the city remains essential to the success, sorry, to their success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: These introductions improve city FEP's voucher administrations by standardizing the unit inspection process, establishing clear limits and application timelines,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: mandating reporting on how long it takes for voucher recipients to secure and move into stable housing, ensure voucher payments are made to landlords on time, and creating a portal for more efficient program administration and documentation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: However, we need reassurance that the HRA will implement these processes according to legislation, thereby making the process of applying for, receiving, and securing housing with city FEPs increasingly clear, transparent, and efficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: Our written testimony provides additional details on HSU's evidence-based advocacy in support of these bills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Pepper Pavlish
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Ann Korczak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York, thanks Council Member Morano for Intro 1424. She says small owners lack administrative staff and a centralized portal to upload documents, manage payments, and enroll in electronic payments would reduce burdens.
chapters.title: Ann Korczak of SPONY testifies on landlord portal bill for small owners

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: My name is Anne Korczak, and I serve as the board president of SPONI, the Small Property Owners of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: And we wanted to speak today, or I wanted to speak today, regarding 1424 and to thank Councilmember Morano for introducing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: This bill addresses a problem that many small owners experience regularly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: The city's housing agencies need to bring their technology and administrative systems into the 21st century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: We've seen the value of this approach because just recently, Congress, Councilman Banks introduced 1023, which would help modernize the HPD building registration process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: So the Councilmember Morano's bill applies the same kind of common sense principle to rental assistance programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: Small owners often don't have property managers or administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: And these processes, especially if you're not dealing with the agency regularly, it's very difficult to deal with many of the hurdles that one faces when

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: dealing with placing a voucher tenant into a unit of housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: So the proposed portal would provide a centralized way to upload documents, manage

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: payment and information, enroll in electronic payments, track payments, all these things would just really lighten the administrative load for small housing providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: So again, we thank Councilman Marano and Chair, thank you for this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: I listened to most of the testimony and I think especially the first panel that spoke about their

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: firsthand experiences with challenges and dealing with the programs was really very moving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak
utterances.text: And I hope that, you know, some of the changes that you're discussing here today can help the process for them as well as the members of my organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ann Korchak

chapters.summary: Miranda DeNovo, who has lived experience of homelessness, describes helping a friend who has been homeless for over two years. She says a referral was lost, a shopping letter promised within two weeks has not arrived after six, and the case was passed between case managers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Miranda DeNovo.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: I don't have a ton to say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: I was doing the nodding in the back to all of this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: So mostly just wanted to add some specific examples about timelines that I've experienced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Like the gentleman who spoke, whose name I didn't catch, I have lived experience of homelessness and have just kind of fallen into like trying to help my friends because as everybody has said, it's pretty impossible to navigate this if you don't

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Was going to say just as like an example of timelines, a friend that I have been trying to support for, they've been homeless for almost two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: The most recent engagement with Homebase started in June of this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Actually, I think it was before that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: So some amount of weeks or months before that, we put in a referral.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: We heard back from the referral in June, did the two eligibility interviews, and then at some point last month we're told, sorry, we submitted the documents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Some way last month we're told that this person would receive a shopping letter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Within two weeks, it's now been, I think, about six.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Part of what seems to be happening is that the case has been passed through at least a couple of different case managers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: And so I finally did get a call from the case manager last week, and it had just been on her desk, and she hadn't had a chance to look at it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: I'm like, that's not even her fault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: That's a staffing thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: But she just truly, I don't think, had even opened the file until I got on the phone with her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: And then now the shopping letter is hinging on, I think,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: some piece of documentation that we submitted that she just said, I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: I've never seen this particular documentation of the eviction before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: I have to ask my supervisor, but like, who knows how much longer it's going to be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Um, before this first, like this, this interaction that's actually led to maybe a shopping letter coming someday soon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: Um, the very first time that we tried to submit a referral was over a year ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Miranda DeNovo
utterances.text: They lost the referral, had to submit a new one three months later.

summary: The Committee on General Welfare held a hearing on five CityFHEPS reform bills covering habitability inspections, lease-up reporting, application response times, rental assistance payment timing, and a landlord portal.

DSS Commissioner Erin Dalton and HRA officials testified about current CityFHEPS operations, pilot inspection changes, processing improvements, payment schedules, and concerns with bill timelines and mandates.

Public testimony from voucher holders, providers, and advocates highlighted long waits, lost apartments, uninhabitable units, Homebase bottlenecks, payment delays, and support for the legislative package.
